column2: And in her mind the goddess grey-eyed Athena put it,
to the daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope,
to set the bow for the suitors and the grey iron
in the halls of Odysseus, as contest prizes and the beginning of slaughter.
She climbed the high stair of her house,
and took in her stout hand a well-curved key,
fair, of bronze; and the handle was of ivory.
She went with her women attendants to the storeroom
at the far end; there lay the treasures of the lord,
bronze and gold and much-wrought iron.
There lay the back-bent bow and the quiver
that holds arrows, and in it were many grievous arrows,
gifts which a guest-friend gave him, having met him in Lacedaemon,
Iphitus, son of Eurytus, like the immortals.
The two met each other in Messene
in the house of wise Ortilochus. Odysseus
had come about a debt, which all the people owed him;
for sheep from Ithaca the Messenian men had carried off
in many-benched ships, three hundred, and the shepherds.
For these Odysseus came on an embassy, a long journey,
being a boy; for his father and other elders sent him forth.
And Iphitus came seeking horses, which had been lost to him,
twelve mares, and under them hardy mules;
which later became his death and fate,
when he came to the son of Zeus, the stout-hearted,
the man Heracles, who knew great deeds,
who killed him, though he was a guest, in his own house,
pitiless, and he did not respect the gods' vengeance nor the table
which he himself had set before him; then he killed him too,
and kept the strong-hoofed horses himself in his halls.
Seeking them, he met Odysseus, and gave him the bow,
which great Eurytus once carried, and which he left to his son
as he was dying in the high halls.
And Odysseus gave him a sharp sword and a stout spear,
the beginning of a close guest-friendship; but they did not
come to know each other at table; for before that the son of Zeus killed
Iphitus, son of Eurytus, like the immortals,
who had given him the bow. And this godly Odysseus never,
going to war on the black ships,
took, but it lay in the halls as a memorial of his dear guest-friend,
and he carried it in his own land.
And when she, the divine one among women, came to the storeroom,
and stepped on the oak threshold, which once a carpenter
planed skilfully and made straight to the line,
and fitted the posts, and set the shining doors,
at once she quickly loosed the strap from the ring,
and put in the key, and shot back the bolts of the doors
aiming straight; and they bellowed like a bull
grazing in a meadow; so loud bellowed the fair doors
struck by the key, and they flew open for her quickly.
And she went onto the high platform; there the chests
stood, and in them fragrant clothes lay.
From there stretching up she took the bow from its peg
with the case itself, which shone around it.
And sitting down there, placing it on her knees,
she wept very shrilly, and took out the bow of her lord.
And she, when she had taken her fill of tearful lament,
went to the hall to the noble suitors,
holding in her hand the back-bent bow and the quiver
that holds arrows; and in it were many grievous arrows.
And with her the handmaids carried a chest, where iron
lay in plenty and bronze, the prizes of that lord.
And when she, the divine one among women, came to the suitors,
she stood by the post of the strongly built roof,
holding before her cheeks her shining veil;
and a faithful handmaid stood on either side of her.
And at once she spoke among the suitors and said a word:

Hear me, proud suitors, who have used this house
69	to eat and drink continually
70	while its master has been gone a long time; and you could make
71	no other pretext for your talk,
72	but in your eagerness to marry me and make me wife.
73	But come, suitors, since this contest is shown:
74	for I will set the great bow of godly Odysseus;
75	and whoever most easily strings the bow in his hands
76	and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes,
77	with him I shall go, leaving this house,
78	my wedded home, very beautiful, full of livelihood,
79	which I think I shall remember even in a dream.
So she spoke, and bade Eumaeus, the godly swineherd,
set the bow for the suitors and the grey iron.
Weeping, Eumaeus received it and put it down;
and the cowherd wept in another place, when he saw the lord's bow.
And Antinous rebuked them, and spoke a word and called by name:

Foolish country men, thinking only of the day,
86	ah wretches, why do you shed tears, and stir the heart
87	of the woman in her breast? whose heart besides
88	lies in pains, since she has lost her dear husband.
89	But sit and feast in silence, or go outside
90	and weep, leaving the bows right here,
91	a contest for the suitors that will not be easy; for I do not think
92	this well-polished bow is easily strung.
93	For among all these there is no such man
94	as Odysseus was; I saw him myself,
95	for I remember, though I was still a child.
So he spoke, and in his breast his spirit hoped
to string the cord and shoot through the iron.
But he was to be the first to taste an arrow
from the hands of blameless Odysseus, whom then he dishonoured,
sitting in the halls, and urged on all his comrades.
And among them spoke the sacred might of Telemachus:

Oh, truly Zeus the son of Kronos has made me witless;
103	my dear mother says, wise though she is,
104	that she will go with another, leaving this house;
105	and I laugh and am pleased with my witless heart.
106	But come, suitors, since this contest is shown,
107	a woman such as there is not now in the Achaean land,
108	neither in holy Pylos nor in Argos nor in Mycenae,
109	nor in Ithaca itself nor in the dark mainland;
110	and you yourselves know this; why must I praise my mother?
111	But come, do not draw it out with excuses, nor longer
112	turn away from stringing the bow, that we may see.
113	And I myself too would try the bow;
114	and if I string it and shoot through the iron,
115	my lady mother would not, to my grief, leave this house
116	going with another, when I am left behind,
117	being now able to take up my father's fair prizes.
He spoke, and from his shoulders he put off his purple cloak,
springing upright, and put off his sharp sword from his shoulders.
First he set up the axes, digging a trench
one long one for all, and made it straight to the line,
and stamped the earth about; and wonder seized all who saw
how well-ordered he set them; for he had never seen it before.
And he went and stood on the threshold and tried the bow.
Three times he made it quiver, eager to draw it,
three times he let go his strength, hoping in his heart
to string the cord and shoot through the iron.
And now he would have strung it, drawing it with force the fourth time,
but Odysseus shook his head, and held him back, eager though he was.
And among them again spoke the sacred might of Telemachus:

Oh, truly I shall be even a coward and weakling hereafter,
132	or I am too young and do not yet trust my hands
133	to defend myself against a man, when someone first grows angry.
134	But come, you who are stronger than I in might,
135	try the bow, and let us finish the contest.
So saying he put the bow from him on the ground,
leaning it against the close-fitted, well-polished doors,
and the swift arrow he leaned there against the fair ring,
and sat down again on the chair from which he had risen.
And among them spoke Antinous, son of Eupeithes:

Rise up in order, all comrades, from left to right,
142	beginning from the place where the wine-pourer pours.
So spoke Antinous, and the speech pleased them.
And Leiodes was the first to rise, son of Oenops,
who was their soothsayer, and by the fair mixing-bowl
always sat in the innermost corner; and wanton deeds
were hateful to him alone, and he was indignant at all the suitors;
he then first took the bow and the swift arrow.
And he went and stood on the threshold and tried the bow,
and he did not string it; for before that he wearied his hands drawing it,
soft and unworn; and he spoke among the suitors:

Friends, I am not stringing it; let another take it.
153	For this bow will rob many of the best men
154	of spirit and life, since it is much better
155	to die than to live and miss that for whose sake we always
156	gather here, waiting every day.
157	Now one hopes in his mind and longs
158	to marry Penelope, Odysseus' wife.
159	But when he has tried the bow and seen it,
160	let him then woo some other of the fair-robed Achaean women
161	with wooing-gifts, seeking her; and she then
162	would marry whoever gives most and comes as destined.
So he spoke, and put the bow from him,
leaning it against the close-fitted, well-polished doors,
and the swift arrow he leaned there against the fair ring,
and sat down again on the chair from which he had risen.
And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word and called by name:

Leiodes, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth,
169	dread and grievous,—I am indignant to hear it—
170	if this bow will indeed rob the best men
171	of spirit and life, because you cannot string it.
172	For your lady mother did not bear you such
173	as to be a drawer of the bow and of arrows;
174	but others will soon string it, the noble suitors.
So he spoke, and bade Melanthius, the goatherd of goats:

Come now, kindle a fire in the halls, Melantheus,
177	and set beside it a great seat and a fleece on it,
178	and bring a great round cake of the fat that is inside,
179	that we young men, warming it and rubbing it with grease,
180	may try the bow and finish the contest.
So he spoke, and Melanthius at once kindled the unwearied fire,
and bringing a seat set it beside it and a fleece on it,
and brought a great round cake of the fat that was inside;
with this the young men warmed it and tried; but could not
string it, and were far short of the strength.
Antinous still held back, and godlike Eurymachus,
leaders of the suitors; they were in excellence by far the best.
And the two went out of the house together,
the cowherd and the swineherd of godly Odysseus;
and after them godly Odysseus himself came out of the house.
But when they were outside the doors and the courtyard,
he spoke to them and addressed them with gentle words:

Cowherd, and you, swineherd, shall I say a word,
194	or keep it myself? My spirit bids me say it.
195	What sort of men would you be to defend Odysseus, if from somewhere he came
196	quite suddenly like this and some god brought him?
197	Would you defend the suitors or Odysseus?
198	Tell me as your heart and spirit bid you.
Then the cowherd spoke to him in turn:
And in the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods
that wise Odysseus might return to his own house.
But when he knew their mind truly,
again he answered them and spoke:

Here inside is this man, myself; having suffered many evils
208	I have come in the twentieth year to my native land.
209	And I know that I have come desired by you two
210	alone of the servants; of the others I have heard none
211	praying that I should come back home again.
212	To you two, as it will be, I will tell the truth:
213	if a god by my hand subdues the noble suitors,
214	I shall bring wives for you both and give you possessions
215	and houses built near mine; and then
216	to Telemachus you two shall be comrades and brothers.
217	But come, I shall show you another clear sign,
218	that you may know me well and be convinced in your hearts,
219	the scar, which once a boar struck me with a white tusk
220	when I went to Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.
So saying he pulled the rags away from the great scar.
And the two, when they had seen it and noted each thing well,
wept, throwing their arms about wise Odysseus,
and kissed him lovingly on the head and shoulders;
and in the same way Odysseus kissed their heads and hands.
And as they wept the light of the sun would have set,
had not Odysseus himself held them back and spoken:

Cease from weeping and lament, lest someone see
229	coming out of the hall, and tell also inside.
230	But go in one by one, not all together,
231	I first, and you after; and let this be the sign:
232	all the others, as many as are noble suitors,
233	will not allow me to be given the bow and quiver;
234	but you, godly Eumaeus, bringing the bow through the house
235	place it in my hands, and tell the women
236	to close the doors of the hall, tightly fitted,
237	and if anyone hears groaning or din inside
238	of men within our walls, let them not
239	rush out, but stay there silent at their work.
240	And to you, godly Philoetius, I give charge of the courtyard doors,
241	to close them with the bar, and quickly throw a rope on them.
So saying he went into the well-inhabited house;
then he went and sat on the seat from which he had risen;
and in went the two servants of godly Odysseus too.
And Eurymachus was now turning the bow in his hands,
warming it this way and that at the fire's blaze; but even so
he could not string it, and he groaned greatly in his glorious heart;
and, vexed, he spoke a word and called by name:

Oh, truly I have grief, both for myself and for all.
250	Not so much for the marriage do I lament, grieved though I am;
251	there are many other Achaean women, some in sea-girt
252	Ithaca itself, and some in other cities;
253	but if we are so far short in strength
254	of godlike Odysseus, that we cannot string
255	the bow; it is a shame even for future men to hear.
Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke to him in turn:

Eurymachus, it will not be so; you yourself know it.
258	For today in the district is the feast of the god,
259	holy; who would bend bows? But set them down
260	quietly; and the axes, even if we leave them all
261	standing; for I think no one will carry them off,
262	coming into the hall of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
263	But come, let the wine-pourer begin the cups with a first pouring,
264	that having poured libations we may put down the curved bows;
265	and at dawn bid Melanthius, the goatherd of goats,
266	to bring goats, which are by far the best of all the herds,
267	that having laid thigh-pieces for Apollo of the famous bow
268	we may try the bow and finish the contest.
So spoke Antinous, and the speech pleased them.
And for them heralds poured water over their hands,
and youths filled the mixing-bowls with drink,
and served all, beginning with the cups.
And when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their spirit wished,
among them, planning guile, spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Hear me, suitors of the famous queen,
276	that I may say what the spirit in my breast bids me.
277	Eurymachus above all and godlike Antinous
278	I beg, since this too he said in due measure,
279	for now leave the bow, and commit it to the gods;
280	and at dawn the god will give victory to whom he wishes.
281	But come, give me the well-polished bow, that among you
282	I may test my hands and strength, whether I still have
283	the might that once was in my supple limbs,
284	or whether wandering and neglect have already destroyed it.
So he spoke, and they all were exceedingly indignant,
fearing that he would string the well-polished bow.
And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word and called by name:

Ah wretched stranger, you have no wits, not even a little;
289	are you not content to feast at your ease among us overweening men,
290	and are not deprived of the feast, but listen
291	to our talk and speech? No other stranger
292	and beggar hears our talk.
293	Honey-sweet wine wounds you, which harms others too,
294	whoever takes it greedily and does not drink in measure.
295	Wine it was that bewildered even the Centaur, famous Eurytion,
296	in the hall of great-hearted Peirithous,
297	when he came to the Lapiths; and when he had bewildered his wits with wine,
298	in madness he did evil through the house of Peirithous;
299	grief seized the heroes, and out through the porch to the door
300	they sprang up and dragged him, and cut off his ears with pitiless bronze
301	and his nostrils; and he, bewildered in his wits,
302	went off bearing his own folly with a foolish heart.
303	From that came strife between the Centaurs and men,
304	but for himself first he found evil, being heavy with wine.
305	So for you too I announce great calamity, if you string
306	the bow; for you will meet with no kindness
307	in our district, but at once in a black ship
308	to king Echetus, the harmer of all mortals,
309	we shall send you; and from there you will not be saved; but sit quietly
310	and drink, and do not quarrel with younger men.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

Antinous, it is not good nor just to slight
313	the guests of Telemachus, whoever comes to this house;
314	do you hope, if the stranger trusting in his hands and his own strength
315	strings the great bow of Odysseus,
316	that he will take me home and make me his wife?
317	Not even he himself hoped this in his breast;
318	and let none of you, grieving in heart for this,
319	feast here, since it is not at all fitting.
Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered her:

Daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope,
322	we do not think this man will take you; it is not fitting;
323	but we are ashamed of the talk of men and women,
324	lest some day someone else of the Achaeans, a baser man, say:
325	'Truly much worse men woo the wife of a blameless man,
326	and cannot string the well-polished bow;
327	but some other beggar, a wanderer who came,
328	easily strung the bow and shot through the iron.'
329	So they will say, and that would be a reproach to us.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

Eurymachus, it is in no way possible to be of good repute
332	in the district for those who dishonour and devour the house
333	of a noble man; why do you make this a reproach?
334	This stranger is very big and well-built,
335	and claims to be born the son of a good father.
336	But come, give him the well-polished bow, that we may see.
337	For thus I will say, and it shall be accomplished:
338	if he strings it, and Apollo grants him glory,
339	I shall clothe him in a cloak and tunic, fair clothes,
340	and give him a sharp javelin, a defender against dogs and men,
341	and a two-edged sword; and I shall give sandals for his feet,
342	and send him wherever his heart and spirit bid.
Then prudent Telemachus answered her:

My mother, of the Achaeans no one has more right than I
345	to give the bow or refuse it, to whom I wish,
346	neither those who rule over rocky Ithaca,
347	nor those in the islands toward horse-feeding Elis;
348	of these no one shall force me against my will, if I wish
349	even to give these bows outright to the stranger to carry away.
350	But go into the house and attend to your own works,
351	the loom and distaff, and bid your handmaids
352	go about their work; the bow will be for the men's care,
353	for all, and above all for me; for the power in the house is mine.
She, amazed, went back to the house;
for she laid the prudent word of her son in her heart.
And having gone up to the upper chamber with her women attendants
she then wept for Odysseus, her dear husband, till on her
grey-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep on her eyelids.
But the godly swineherd took the curved bow and carried it;
and the suitors all shouted at him in the halls;
and thus one of the overbearing young men would say:

Where are you carrying the curved bow, you wretched swineherd,
363	you wanderer? Soon the swift dogs will eat you among your swine,
364	alone away from men, whom you reared, if Apollo
365	and the other immortal gods are gracious to us.
So they said; and he put it down where he was,
frightened, because many shouted in the halls.
And Telemachus from the other side called out threateningly:

Father, carry the bow on; soon you will not do well to obey all,
370	lest, though younger, I drive you to the fields,
371	pelting you with stones; for I am stronger in might.
372	Would that I were as much stronger than all the suitors
373	who are in the house, in hands and in strength;
374	then I would soon send some one of them away in disgrace
375	from our house, since they devise evils.
So he spoke, and all the suitors laughed sweetly at him,
and relaxed from their harsh anger
at Telemachus; and the swineherd carrying the bow through the house
standing by put it in the hands of wise Odysseus.
And calling out the nurse Eurycleia he said to her:

Telemachus bids you, wise Eurycleia,
382	close the doors of the hall, tightly fitted;
383	and if anyone hears groaning or din inside
384	of men within our walls, let her not
385	rush out, but stay there silent at her work.
So he spoke, and her word was wingless,
and she locked the doors of the well-inhabited halls.
And silently Philoetius leapt out of the house,
and then closed the doors of the well-fenced courtyard.
There lay under the portico the cable of a double-curved ship,
of papyrus, with which he fastened the doors, and went in himself;
then he went and sat on the seat from which he had risen,
looking at Odysseus. And he was already handling the bow,
turning it every way, testing it this way and that,
lest worms might have eaten the horns while the lord was away.
And thus one would say, looking at his neighbour:

Truly he is some connoisseur and rogue of bows;
398	or perhaps such a one lies at his own home,
399	or he is eager to make one, the way in his hands
400	he turns it this way and that, the wanderer skilled in evils.
And another of the overbearing young men said:

Would that he might meet with as much profit
403	as he will ever be able to string this.
So spoke the suitors; but Odysseus of many wiles,
as soon as he had lifted the great bow and looked it over on every side,
as when a man skilled in the lyre and song
easily stretches a string round a new peg,
fastening on both sides the twisted sheep-gut,
so without effort Odysseus strung the great bow.
And taking it in his right hand he tried the string;
and it sang beautifully beneath, like a swallow in voice.
And great grief came on the suitors, and the colour of all
changed; and Zeus thundered loudly, showing signs;
and the much-enduring godly Odysseus rejoiced
that the son of Kronos of crooked counsel sent him a portent.
And he took a swift arrow, which lay beside him on the table
bare; and the others lay inside the hollow quiver,
which the Achaeans were soon to taste.
This he took and set on the bridge, and drew the string and notches,
right from the chair where he sat, and shot the arrow
aiming straight, and did not miss the first ring
of all the axes, and right through and out
went the bronze-weighted arrow; and he spoke to Telemachus:

Telemachus, the stranger sitting in your halls does not shame you,
425	nor did I miss the mark nor for long
426	did I toil at stringing the bow; my strength is still firm,
427	not as the suitors, dishonouring me, taunt.
428	But now it is time for supper to be prepared for the Achaeans
429	in the light, and afterwards to play otherwise
430	with song and lyre; for these are the accompaniments of a feast.
He spoke, and nodded with his brows; and Telemachus
girded on his sharp sword, dear son of godly Odysseus,
and took his spear in his dear hand, and close by him
beside the chair he stood, armed with gleaming bronze.
